title: Bits: Single Number (XOR Cancels Pairs)
oneLiner: Every value appears twice except one: XOR everything together and the pairs cancel, leaving the single one.
keyTakeaway: XOR has three properties that make this work: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and order doesn't matter. So XOR-ing the whole array pairs every duplicate with its twin (giving 0) and leaves the lone value. O(n) time, O(1) space, where a hash set or counting map would need O(n) memory.
explanation:
Given a non-empty integer array where every element appears exactly twice except for one, find that one. Use O(n) time and O(1) extra space. For [4, 1, 2, 1, 2] the answer is 4.

A hash set would work (add a value the first time, remove it the second, and one value is left over) but that's O(n) memory. Sorting and checking neighbours is O(n log n). The bit trick needs neither.

XOR (exclusive or, ^ in both C# and Python) compares two numbers bit by bit and gives 1 where the bits DIFFER and 0 where they match. That means x ^ x = 0 for any x (every bit matches itself), x ^ 0 = x (XOR with 0 changes nothing), and a ^ b ^ a = b because XOR is commutative and associative: you can reorder and regroup it freely. XOR every element into one accumulator starting at 0. Mentally rearrange so twins sit together: each pair becomes 0, and 0 ^ single = single.

Another way to see it: look at one bit position at a time. Each pair contributes its bit twice, which flips that position twice and leaves it as it was. Only the single number's bits flip an odd number of times, so they are what's left.

Negative numbers work unchanged. In C# an int is 32 bits in two's complement, where -k is stored as the bit pattern of 2^32 - k, and XOR just works on those bits. Python ints behave as if they had infinitely many sign bits, and XOR still cancels pairs exactly, so -2 comes out as -2.

The visualization XORs [5, 3, 5, 6, 3] as 4-bit rows. The bottom row is the running XOR.

acc ^= 5: 0000 ^ 0101 = 0101 (acc = 5). Each 1 in 5 flips that bit of acc.
acc ^= 3: 0101 ^ 0011 = 0110 (acc = 6). Each 1 in 3 flips that bit of acc.
acc ^= 5: 0110 ^ 0101 = 0011 (acc = 3). Each 1 in 5 flips that bit of acc.
acc ^= 6: 0011 ^ 0110 = 0101 (acc = 5). Each 1 in 6 flips that bit of acc.
acc ^= 3: 0101 ^ 0011 = 0110 (acc = 6). Each 1 in 3 flips that bit of acc.
Done: acc = 6. Both 5s and both 3s flipped their bits twice, which cancels; only 6's bits are left.

recognitionSignals: "Every element appears twice except one" (or an even number of times except one).
O(1) extra space ruling out a hash set, on a problem that is really about counting occurrences.
Pairs that should cancel out: XOR is the operation where combining something with itself gives nothing.
gotchas: Start the accumulator at 0, the XOR identity, not at nums[0] plus a loop that XORs nums[0] again.
It only works for "twice" (or any even count). If others appear three times, count each bit position modulo 3 instead.
^ is XOR in C# and Python, not exponentiation. Powers are Math.Pow in C# and ** in Python.
confusableWith: Hash Map counting solves the general "which value appears an odd number of times" problem with O(n) space.
Missing Number (this track) uses the same cancellation, XOR-ing the indexes 0..n against the values.

complexity.note: One XOR per element into a single accumulator, versus O(n) space for a hash set.
